Abstract: Two-dimensional shallow water equations (2D-SWEs) are essential to watershed flood control, river and lake ecological management, and digital twin development. However, model uncertainty can significantly reduce the accuracy of simulation results. Model structure, including spatial discretization and numerical schemes, is one of the key uncertainty sources. This study conducted an uncertainty analysis of 2D-SWEs using mesh independence, computational efficiency, and computational accuracy as evaluation criteria. It investigated differences in model structure and computational characteristics and further explored the structural causes for these computational differences. The results indicated that all mesh types in Delft3D FM exhibited excellent mesh independence, whereas in MIKE 21 FM, triangular meshes demonstrated better mesh independence than quadrilateral meshes. Compared with the boundary conditions involving upstream and downstream discharge, the boundary conditions including upstream discharge and downstream water level can reduce model uncertainty but may also mask underlying model issues. The computational efficiency of unstructured triangular meshes (UTM) was significantly lower than that of unstructured quadrilateral meshes (UQM) and hybrid meshes (UQM_UTM). Specifically, the computational time of MIKE 21 FM using UTM was 1.54 times that of MIKE 21 FM using UQM and 3.24 times that of Delft3D FM using UQM. All combinations of models and mesh types accurately simulated the spatiotemporal evolution of flow. However, Manning's coefficient for quadrilateral meshes in MIKE 21 FM differed significantly from other combinations. This is primarily because the numerical scheme of MIKE 21 FM is better suited for triangular meshes, whereas that of Delft3D FM is suitable for quadrilateral meshes. Overall, model uncertainty is influenced by boundary conditions, numerical schemes, mesh types, and the coupled effects of various factors. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V. on behalf of Hohai University. Title: Towards Practical Digital Twin Construction Systems
Source title: Proceedings of the International Symposium on Automation and Robotics in Construction
Affiliations: Seskin Virtual Construction Laboratory, Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, Israel
Authors with affiliations: Yeung T., Seskin Virtual Construction Laboratory, Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, Israel; Sacks R., Seskin Virtual Construction Laboratory, Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, Israel
Abstract: Building construction projects are socio-technical production systems in which variance, uncertainty and unpredictable events are the norm. Such systems need short-cycle Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) loops to detect anomalies in production flow as early as possible so that remedial actions can be evaluated and well-informed decisions made. This is the goal of Digital Twin Construction (DTC). We define practical DTC as a minimal coherent system that captures a project’s current status, compares the status to design and planning intent, analyses variance, predicts the outcomes of possible interventions, and thus informs specific managerial decisions at the required cadence. The approach characterizes managerial decisions by autonomy, fidelity, and scope, and proposes five degrees of implementation as system capability configurations for incremental development. This contributes an actionable basis for specifying and incrementally implementing DTC systems that deliver decision value early while maintaining a clear pathway toward more advanced implementations. © 2026 International Association on Automation and Robotics in Construction. Abstract: Smart maintenance service systems increasingly rely on advanced diagnostics to support servitization models that deliver reliability and availability as managed outcomes. This paper introduces a Quantum Computing-as-a-Service (QCaaS) approach for diagnostic intelligence by integrating Bayesian Network (BN) learning with digital twin (DT) representations. BN structure learning, intervention analysis, and DT model fusion are formulated as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems and solved using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) implemented in Qiskit Aer. A hybrid workflow connects BN-to-QUBO encoding, DT data pipelines, and QCaaS-based optimization services. Benchmark experiments demonstrate that quantuminspired methods demonstrate improved structure accuracy and runtime scalability compared to classical solvers, positioning QCaaS as a scalable computational capability that enhances fault reasoning, uncertainty modeling, and decision support in digital-twin-enabled maintenance servitization ecosystems. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The article addresses the challenges associated with the Product-as-a-Service (PaaS) concept in the context of the circular economy. The use of simulation technologies within this concept can accelerate the adoption of circular economy principles in companies. It enables faster modelling and optimisation of value-retention processes such as remanufacturing and refurbishment. The aim of the paper is to propose a simulation approach that allows engineers to develop simulation models (digital twins) in the same way they design and redesign closed-loop manufacturing systems. A further objective is to highlight the specific requirements for testing such simulation models and for sizing planned digital-twin projects. The article presents the development of a hybrid model that combines discrete piece-flow for remanufacturing with mass flow (in kilograms) for recycling, using household appliances as an example and identifying sources of uncertainty that affect the organisation of PaaS processes, particularly remanufacturing and recycling. The main contribution is the development of a hybrid simulation approach based on operations in the PaaS domain, i.e. closed-loop manufacturing with the 6R framework, and the application of the COSMIC methodology to size simulation projects. The article also discusses methods for simulation modelling of individual sources of uncertainty and uses an operation-based simulation method instead of conventional discrete-event simulation. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) generation in urban and utility-scale installations has increased the need for reliable global maximum power point tracking (GMPPT) solutions in complicated and fast-changing partially shaded situations. Traditional MPPT controllers struggle to grasp multi-peak Voltage power landscapes shaded by clouds, neighboring structures, vegetation, and soiling patterns. As PV adoption rises, momentary tracking failures waste energy and degrade power electronics. Deterministic scanning, meta-heuristic, and data-driven optimizers focus on global peak placement but consider partial shading opaque disturbance. Long convergence durations, transitory energy loss, noise and sensor bias sensitivity, or unstable global maximum oscillations are common. PV systems cannot use many learning-based methods because they lack systematic validation under fault and uncertainty situations. To solve these constraints, this research presents a fully integrated, machine-learning-driven GMPPT system that explicitly models, exploits, and analyzes partial shading dynamics utilizing a five-stage analytical process. It comprises of spectral-physics informed shading map (SPIN Map) that infers latent shading states, a differentiable digital twin uses this shading context to build a continuously calibrated multi-peak PV power to reliably predict candidate global maxima with quantified uncertainty. Further, GMPPT is handled as a contextual bandit issue, selecting candidate regions that maximize expected power gain and minimize exploration induced energy loss, and constrained reinforcement learning controller explicitly compensates for noise and rapid irradiance transients to track the global optimum steadily with negligible oscillations. Over earlier GMPPT techniques, the proposed method decreases energy loss during shade transitions and improves convergence speed, tracking efficiency, and resilience. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A Hybrid Machine Learning and Mathematical Optimisation Framework for Energy Consumption Prediction in Smart Sustainable Systems
Source title: 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Engineering and Innovation, AISEI 2026
Affiliations: Jadara University, Faculty of Science And, Mathematics Department, Jordan

Abstract: Operational decarbonisation in smart sustainable systems depends on reliable short-horizon decisions under uncertainty. Such decisions remain high-leverage for buildings because of their large share of global energy use and emissions [3], [4]. The paper presents a hybrid framework combining day-ahead consumption prediction with a peak-aware mathematical scheduling layer. This predictor applies gradient-boosted regression to capture the nonlinear interactions of temporal structure, exogenous drivers, and lagged consumption. Adaptive residual quantiles on a rolling window measure uncertainty and form lower and upper envelopes that are responsive to drift in behaviour and regime. The optimization layer developed for PV-battery dispatch is linear program which minimizes energy cost penalizes peak grid import subject to battery dynamics power limits and state-of-charge limits. A strong variant is scheduled against the upper envelope in order to reduce peak violations in the event of forecast error. The suggested predictor makes a 4.06 kW RMSE persistence; 8.72 kW; ridge; 5.96 on a 15-minute digital-twin dataset. The mean cost is reduced by 2.64 % and peak import reduced by 11.13 % over the period of 14 days when the solution is coupled optimised, while robust planning reduces the peak-limit exceedance by half. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The increasing use of Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) systems for high-precision dimensional metrology in industrial environments demands not only accurate data but also reliable quantification of measurement uncertainty. Traditional methods, such as ISO 15530-3 and the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM), require extensive experimental effort and are often directly applicable only to prismatic geometries, limiting their use for novel geometries or conditions. Freeform geometries are increasingly applied in manufacturing for topological and functional optimization, yet conventional CMM uncertainty evaluation methods are tailored to primitive geometries, restricting their applicability. This work proposes a novel data-driven framework that leverages machine learning (ML) prediction models trained on actual CMM measurement data and integrates an uncertainty analysis to provide predictions with metrological trustworthiness. The approach begins with collecting an extensive dataset, through a factorial design structured by design of experiment (DOE), from tactile CMM measurements on calibrated artefacts with prismatic and freeform geometries. Influential factors such as sampling density, measurement strategy, probe configuration, and alignment are considered as model inputs. A supervised ML algorithm is trained to predict measurement outcomes (e.g., geometric deviations, form errors) as a function of these parameters. Unlike classical statistical models, the ML model captures complex interactions among process parameters and machine behaviour. Uncertainty is evaluated using a statistical resampling approach based on bootstrap methodology. Multiple bootstrapped samples are generated, and the ML model is retrained for each, producing an ensemble of prediction models. The variability in coefficients and outputs provides estimates of standard and expanded uncertainty in accordance with GUM principles. The framework bridges conventional DOE-based metrological modelling and modern data-driven methods. It enables quantification of ML prediction uncertainty for CMM processes, supporting virtual validation, metrological digital twins, and bridging towards complex measurement tasks' error compensation strategies. © 2026 EUSPEN. Source title: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
Affiliations: Politecnico di Torino, Department of Electronics and Telecommunications, Turin, 10129, Italy; NTT Network Innovation Laboratories, Kanagawa, Yokosuka, 239-0847, Japan; NEC Laboratories America, Princeton, 08540, NJ, United States

Abstract: Polarization-dependent loss (PDL) makes the post-equalization signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of a coherent optical lightpath stochastic, with an outage-relevant lower tail that depends on the longitudinal interleaving of PDL elements and amplified-spontaneous-emission (ASE) noise sources. Under a finite-hinge representation, the inverse-SNR is a weighted sum of correlated exponentials of a random walk, whose exact evaluation is too costly for repeated quality-of-transmission assessment in an optical network digital twin (ONDT), where physical-layer models are continuously combined with network data to predict transmission feasibility and support network operation. We model the PDL magnitude of each element through a Maxwell prior in dB and compare five efficient approximations: gamma moment matching, recursive moment-matched lognormal, correlated Fenton–Wilkinson lognormal, delta-cumulant log-skew-normal, and third-moment recursive log-skew-normal. Their descriptors can be accumulated element by element or exchanged as a constant-size moment state across vendor and operator domains, while allowing different PDL statistics in different network portions. Monte Carlo validation based on 10^{9} realizations, with N\in \{2,10,40\} and \sigma _{\mathrm {PDL}} from 0.1 to 1.5 dB, shows that no approximation is uniformly best. In the practically relevant sub-1 dB range, the third-moment recursive log-skew-normal model is generally the most accurate global approximation and provides the best overall outage-tail prediction, with outage-probability errors typically within a few tenths of a decade and outage-quantile errors of about 0.2 dB or less. Realistic core–metro and metro–access examples further show that propagation direction, received optical power, and transceiver SNR jointly alter both the reference SNR and the distribution shape. The scope is limited to ASE-dominated links, independent per-element Maxwell priors, and ideal zero-forcing polarization equalization; Kerr nonlinear noise, non-ideal receivers, and correlated or telemetry-conditioned PDL models remain for future work. © 2020 IEEE.

Abstract: The pharmaceutical industry is undergoing rapid change, driven by increasing scientific complexity, stringent regulatory requirements, rising development costs, and shorter time to market. Conventional project management techniques, although foundational, are not sufficient for managing the uncertainty and scale of modern drug development. Artificial intelligence (AI), together with digital platforms, advanced analytics, and automation, is growing as a critical enabler of adaptive, data-driven pharmaceutical project management. This review critically examines current and emerging applications of AI across pharmaceutical project management, spanning research and development, clinical development, Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC), manufacturing, quality, and regulatory affairs. It also evaluates challenges related to data integrity, regulatory acceptance, ethics, and organizational readiness, and highlights future trends such as agile AI-driven management, digital twins, and generative AI. The article provides a future perspective relevant to industry professionals, academics, and policymakers. © 2026 Académie Nationale de Pharmacie.

Abstract: The uncertainty of the soil conditions, non-uniform ageing and the challenge of safe testing of adaptive controllers on live underground assets restrict the use of real-time thermal management of underground electrical networks. This study presents an adaptive electro-thermal network model, a fuzzy cognitive map (FCM) for causal risk aggregation, tabular reinforcement learning and a predictive safety shield to realize closed-loop digital twins. The framework was tested on a repeatable simulation of three thermally coupled XLPE cable circuits with a time resolution of 5 min. Two learning agents were each trained on 100 randomized simulated days and then compared with fixed allocation, threshold control, a one-step FCM controller and temperature-only reinforcement learning under nominal and disturbed sensing and soil conditions over 20 held-out days per condition. When the FCM–SafeRL was applied in nominal conditions, it maintained the maximum conductor temperature at 88.62 ± 0.19 ℃, without ever exceeding 90 ℃, and with 0.41 ± 0.50% unserved energy. It also reduced daily dispatch movement by 79.2% compared with the more conservative one-step FCM controller. There was no thermal-limit violation for FCM–SafeRL in all of the scenarios of high sensor noise, 20% sensor loss, a 25% increase in soil resistance and a compound disturbance (+ 20% soil resistance, 20% sensor loss and 1.0 ℃ sensor noise). These results are useful for the feasibility analysis of the fusion of fuzzy causal-risk reasoning and shielded learning in all of the evaluated simulation scenarios, but do not imply a formal safety guarantee; field calibration and HIL validation still need to be performed. © Akadémiai Kiadó Zrt 2026.

Abstract: The article considers a methodology for intelligent processing of multimodal information based on the regularizing Bayesian approach (RBA) under conditions of uncertainty, small samples, incomplete data, and conceptual instability. The central idea of the work is the formation of a unified trusted loop in which measurement data, expert knowledge, IoT streaming information, and the outputs of generative models are brought to a consistent representation, undergo formal verification, and are evaluated by probabilistic methods. It is shown that the «Infoanalytic 3.0» platform can serve as a practical implementation of such a methodology: it combines tools for data integration, construction of digital twins, decision support, deterministic structuring of unstructured texts, and automatic quality assessment of LLM components. The proposed approach improves the reproducibility, interpretability, and reliability of intelligent systems operating under significant information uncertainty. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: The sentient infrastructure paradigm: a review of novel sensors, digital twins, and AI for civil structural health monitoring
Source title: Sensor Review

Authors with affiliations: Mohammed B., Computer Science Department, Faculty of Science Exact, Tahri Mohammed Bechar University, Bechar, Algeria
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to synthesize the “Sentient Infrastructure” paradigm, a transformative shift from reactive to proactive civil infrastructure management. The author critically analyze the synergistic integration of a sensor “Nervous System, ” a dynamic “Digital Brain” (Digital Twins) and an artificial intelligence (AI) “Cognition Engine, ” supported by a secure Internet of Things “Circulatory System.” By framing these technologies into a bio-inspired, closed-loop architecture, this work provides a holistic blueprint for creating intelligent, self-aware cyber-physical infrastructure capable of autonomous diagnosis, prognosis and adaptive resilience, ultimately paving the way for safer and more sustainable infrastructure management. Design/methodology/approach – This review adopts a systematic, multidisciplinary approach integrating civil engineering, materials science and AI. It synthesizes over 100 recent studies on novel sensors, dynamic digital twins and AI-driven diagnostics to construct a unified *Sentient Infrastructure* framework. The methodology includes comparative analyses of sensing technologies, mathematical modeling of data assimilation using Ensemble Kalman Filters, and evaluation of AI models such as physics-informed and generative neural networks. Additionally, real-world case studies illustrate practical implementations and performance metrics, validating how the integration of sensing, modeling and cognition enables adaptive, real-time and resilient infrastructure management. Findings – The study reveals that integrating advanced sensors, dynamic digital twins and AI-driven cognition transforms infrastructure from passive systems into adaptive, self-aware entities. Novel sensors like TENGs and distributed fiber optics enable dense, continuous monitoring; data assimilation through Ensemble Kalman Filters ensures real-time model fidelity; and physics-informed AI enhances diagnostic accuracy and remaining useful life prediction. Case studies confirm up to 80% improvement in model precision and 99% reduction in damage detection time. Collectively, these technologies establish a closed-loop framework that enables predictive maintenance, operational efficiency and resilient infrastructure management across diverse civil applications. Research limitations/implications – While the Sentient Infrastructure paradigm shows transformative potential, its large-scale deployment faces several limitations. High implementation costs, lack of interoperability standards and uncertainties in long-term sensor durability pose practical challenges. Additionally, the complexity and opacity of AI models raise trust and explainability issues for safety-critical decisions. Data governance, privacy and cybersecurity concerns also remain unresolved. These limitations imply a strong need for interdisciplinary research in federated learning, neuromorphic edge computing and explainable AI to ensure scalable, transparent and secure adoption of sentient infrastructure systems in real-world civil engineering and smart city environments. Practical implications – The Sentient Infrastructure paradigm offers significant practical benefits for engineers, asset managers and policymakers. By integrating self-powered sensors, dynamic digital twins and AI-driven analytics, it enables real-time condition assessment, predictive maintenance and optimized resource allocation. This reduces inspection costs, minimizes downtime and enhances public safety. Case studies demonstrate measurable improvements in model accuracy, early fault detection and lifecycle management. The framework also supports smart city development through system-of-systems integration, allowing coordinated management of bridges, tunnels and utilities. Overall, it provides a scalable pathway toward resilient, data-driven and self-adaptive civil infrastructure systems. Social implications – The Sentient Infrastructure paradigm holds profound social benefits by enhancing the safety, reliability and sustainability of critical public assets. Continuous, intelligent monitoring reduces the risk of catastrophic failures, protecting lives and communities. Predictive maintenance optimizes public spending, freeing resources for social development. Moreover, resilient infrastructure strengthens disaster preparedness and climate adaptability, ensuring uninterrupted mobility and essential services. The integration of explainable AI fosters transparency and public trust in automated decision-making. Ultimately, this paradigm contributes to building smarter, safer and more sustainable cities that improve quality of life and societal resilience. Originality/value – This paper introduces the *Sentient Infrastructure* paradigm as a novel, integrative framework that redefines civil infrastructure as a self-aware cyber-physical system. Unlike prior studies focusing separately on sensors, digital twins or AI, it unifies these domains into a cohesive architecture comprising a “nervous system, ” “digital brain, ” and “cognition engine.” The work’s originality lies in its systems-level synthesis, the introduction of bioinspired analogies for infrastructure intelligence and the use of physics-informed and generative AI for real-time diagnosis and prognosis. It provides a visionary yet practical roadmap for transforming infrastructure management from reactive to predictive and autonomous. © 2026 Emerald Publishing Limited

Title: How AI–Driven Transformation Reshapes Competitiveness in Incumbent Firms

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how firms compete, innovate, and coordinate value creation in increasingly complex economic systems. While contemporary discourse remains largely focused on automation and productivity gains, this chapter examines how AI-driven transformation alters the strategic foundations of incumbent organizations. It develops a framework that distinguishes three stages in the evolution of AI capabilities: algorithmic consolidation, anticipatory integration, and architectural transformation. A longitudinal comparative analysis of five multinational incumbents shows how machine learning, digital twins, and simulation platforms reshape decision-making, business models, and stakeholder coordination. The findings suggest that competitive advantage increasingly depends on embedding anticipatory capabilities into organizational governance and value architectures. In doing so, AI-driven transformation enables firms to align innovation, sustainability objectives, and long-term resilience in environments characterized by systemic uncertainty. © 2027 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Title: A digital twin-enhanced deep metric learning framework for few-shot combustion fault diagnosis in marine diesel engines
Source title: JVC/Journal of Vibration and Control
Affiliations: Logistics Engineering College, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, China
Authors with affiliations: Luo D., Logistics Engineering College, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, China; Geng P., Logistics Engineering College, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, China; Hu X., Logistics Engineering College, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, China
Abstract: Combustion fault diagnosis in marine diesel engines is hindered by scarce labeled fault samples, feature drift under variable operating conditions, and cross-condition distribution shifts. This paper proposes a digital twin (DT)-enhanced deep metric learning framework for few-shot combustion fault diagnosis. A 0D/1D thermodynamic DT model of a Wärtsilä 6L20 marine diesel engine is built in MATLAB/Simulink, and three typical combustion faults are parametrically injected. Five physics-informed thermodynamic features augment raw multi-sensor signals. A 1D-CNN Siamese network with a joint triplet–center loss maps input signals into a 128-dimensional embedding space optimized for inter-class separation and intra-class compactness. A two-stage training strategy pre-trains on abundant DT-generated source-condition data and fine-tunes only fully connected layers on K target-condition samples per class. Under a cycle-level, leakage-free data splitting protocol, the proposed joint-loss method achieves 87.05% ± 5.14 pp (mean ± standard deviation over 10 runs) accuracy at K = 20, while a triplet-only ablation reaches 90.91%, indicating that the triplet term is the dominant driver of few-shot discrimination. The average accuracy remains 84.43% under combined noise and speed fluctuation interference across 25–100% MCR loads. Ablation, visualization, and GUM-compliant measurement uncertainty studies validate each module. The framework’s primary contribution lies in physics-informed feature augmentation and data-efficient two-stage training rather than a claim of state-of-the-art accuracy; it provides a simulation-based foundation for training diagnostic models when real-vessel fault data are unavailable. © The Author(s) 2026

Title: Phase-Guided Bayesian Model-Based Imputation for Missing Sensor Data in Mass-Spring-Damper Systems
Source title: Conference Record - IEEE Instrumentation and Measurement Technology Conference
Affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States
Authors with affiliations: Bouraima M.O., Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States; Zawodniok M., Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States
Abstract: Missing sensor data severely degrades parameter estimation in dynamic systems. In digital-twin applications for mechanical equipment, gaps in vibration or displacement measurements corrupt phase estimates, causing the virtual twin to diverge from the physical system and undermining both real-time monitoring and predictive-maintenance decisions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Phase-Guided Bayesian Model-Based Imputation (PGMI-Bayesian) that uses a physics-guided two-stage scheme for reconstructing missing samples and refining phase estimation in a mass-spring-damper system. The approach first generates model-consistent estimations and then applies a weak Bayesian shrinkage update. Monte Carlo results show that PGMI-Bayesian consistently achieves lower variance, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Mean Squared Error (MSE) than both observed-only estimation and standard imputation strategies. Although it does not reach the complete-data Cramér-Rao Lower Bound, the method remains well below the Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) CRLB for missingness up to 30%. Entropy analysis further confirms that PGMI-Bayesian produces the lowest-uncertainty reconstructions, demonstrating that physics-guided reconstruction can meaningfully enhance estimator efficiency under missing data. © 2026 IEEE.
